strengths: The paper addresses an important question: how adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while producing a substantial robust generalization gap.

Combining representation complexity with training dynamics is a useful perspective. The local-memorization construction and signal/noise decomposition provide an intuitive mechanism with measurable quantities.

The experiments include MNIST, CIFAR10, synthetic feature trajectories, and input-loss-flatness diagnostics. These illustrate the qualitative phenomenon and help make the proposed explanation understandable.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on (e1,+1) and (-e1,-1), radius δ=1/4, and f_clean(x)=x1+8x2. Assumptions 4.1–4.3 hold: the support is bounded and separated, and the small clean classifier is accurate but nonrobust. With N=D samples, both atoms have empirical frequencies bounded away from zero with high probability. Consequently, vanishing robust training error forces zero robust population error, precluding CGRO. Additional assumptions controlling distributional mass and sample coverage are necessary.

The representation proof has further substantive gaps. Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous f_S by continuous ReLU networks, which is impossible when its jumps remain bounded away from zero. Soft indicators require control of transition regions and classification margins, which is not supplied. Furthermore, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes only; it does not imply the asserted disjointness of every pair of training balls.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robustness under the paper's declared threat model. Definition 5.6 trains against perturbations restricted to the signal direction in the meaningful patch, whereas Definition 3.3 measures robust training error over the entire norm ball. Small restricted-adversarial loss does not imply small full-ball robust training error. Appendix E.12 makes this unsupported inference, leaving a central component of the CGRO conclusion unproved.

The clean-generalization argument in Appendix E.12 uses an incorrect concentration claim: cubic Gaussian projections are not generally sub-Gaussian. The stated bound also neglects correlations between neurons evaluated on the same noise patch. Additionally, an aggregate memorization statistic does not establish the claimed norm of each neuron's noise component. Correct concentration and norm bounds, with explicit dimension and width conditions, are needed to support Theorem 5.9.

The synthetic experiment sets δ=α=10, violating Assumption 5.7's strict δ<α condition. At this radius, the permitted attack can erase the only label-dependent patch, so poor robust generalization does not validate the theorem's separated setting. The image experiments show accuracy gaps and flatness patterns but do not isolate the proposed memorization mechanism. Reproduction and assessment of attack strength are also hindered by insufficient reporting of PGD iterations, step sizes, restarts, complete optimization settings, and variation across runs.

The originality and explanatory role of the lower bound need clarification. Theorem 4.7 is existential over distributions admitting a polynomial-size clean classifier; the linearly separable hard distributions attributed to Li et al. (2022) already belong to this class. The manuscript does not identify a stronger conclusion obtained by this relaxation. Its worst-case representation lower bound is also not shown to apply to the structured distribution analyzed in Section 5 or the image datasets. Overall, the promising conceptual framing does not compensate for the unresolved errors in the principal theoretical claims.
